There was a particular relief in sitting near someone who expected him to have an opinion about a dumpling. He had begun to lose that scale. A call unanswered for twenty minutes could occupy more of his mind than the meal in front of him. Garrett’s ordinary annoyance about a leaking container did not solve anything. It reminded Rei that ordinary problems still existed.
Rei opens the kept storyboard alone. Its crooked miniature roof recalls the work of holding it still, before the page recalls any later loss.
FLASHBACK — High-school lunch break
“Hold the pigeon there,” Marcus said. “No, higher. It has a very important bus to miss.”
Rei looked at the timetable. “This says it arrives yesterday.”
“Public transport with ambition.”
“That's not what ambition means.”
“Fine. Public transport with a serious administrative problem. Hold still.”
The roof slipped. Rei caught it before it flattened the cardboard street.
Marcus lowered his hands. “A very local weather event.”
“You built a roof that doesn't fit.”
“You moved the building.”
“Because the pigeon couldn't get past it.”
For a moment neither spoke. Marcus looked between the pieces, annoyed enough that Rei wondered whether he should offer to start again.
Instead Marcus picked up the pencil.
“If I make the street wider, it stops looking like the place I wanted.”
“Then let it get in the way.”
“What?”
“The pigeon can walk around it.” Rei shifted the little bird along the edge of the building. “It misses the bus. It goes past the places the bus doesn't.”
Marcus watched him move it. Then he leaned over the page.
“Wait. Do that again.”
Rei did.
“Slower.”
“You could say please.”
“Please perform the extremely important pigeon journey again.”
Rei laughed. Marcus was already drawing, tongue briefly caught between his teeth as he concentrated.
“You're changing my whole bit,” Rei said.
“I'm fixing the part where you made it interesting and didn't tell me where it ended.”
“So it was interesting.”
“Don't make me regret saying it.”

They tried the movement again. It took longer than either of them expected. Marcus changed his mind twice and refused to change it a third time. Rei complained, then held the roof where it needed to be.
“You're buying lunch after this.”
“Half my sandwich and a credit bigger than the pigeon.”
“Deal.”
PRESENT DAY

Adult Rei rested his hand beside the drawing. He remembered being hungry and irritated and pleased with their idea. He let all three things remain in the memory. Marcus had been there making decisions, not waiting to become the subject of somebody else's grief.

Back at his own table, Rei thought of a different school afternoon: Marcus returning the borrowed eraser in a paper envelope labelled temporary custody concluded. It had been absurdly formal for a grubby rectangle of rubber. Rei had kept the envelope because someone had taken the trouble to make him laugh without needing him to perform first. He missed the next ridiculous thing Marcus would have wanted him to take seriously.
Emily looked at the storyboard Rei had chosen to bring.
“He could be so stubborn about it.”
Rei glanced up.
She hesitated. “I-I don't mean that badly.”
“No,” he said. “He could.”
Sophie leaned forward without taking the page. “You were both very certain a cardboard bird needed that much discussion.”
“It did.”
“Apparently.”
Rei found himself defending the idea before he remembered he didn't have to. “It wasn't just the bird. He wanted it to feel like a place.”
Emily nodded. “I… I liked listening to him explain things. Even when I didn't know how he got from the first thing to the last.”
“He'd get there,” Rei said.
“Eventually,” Sophie said.
He laughed. The laugh stopped abruptly, leaving him embarrassed by how exposed he felt.
Emily looked down at her hands. “I do that too.”
“What?”
“Laugh. Then feel as though I've forgotten something.”
Rei ran his thumb along the edge of the paper. “Sometimes I feel like I'm being dishonest if I talk about a good day.”
Sophie waited before answering. “I don't think a good day stops having happened.”
“I know. It just feels strange.”
“Yes,” Emily said. “It does.”
Neither rushed to make it feel different. Rei looked at the drawing again and told them how Marcus had refused to widen the street. The disagreement mattered to the story. He left it in.

For a moment they disagreed about which part of the film had been Marcus’s idea. The disagreement felt almost precious. He had existed in each of their lives separately; Rei could not hold every version of him by remembering harder. Emily’s recollection made him smile. Sophie corrected a detail and kept it corrected. Neither asked grief’s permission to remember him as occasionally infuriating.

RD11.title: The empty place on the bench

elements.text: The folded corner of the storyboard caught under Rei’s thumb. Adult hands, his own table, the city outside the window. He knew where he was. The school morning came back anyway.
FLASHBACK — School courtyard, after Marcus’s death

Emily and Sophie were waiting beside the bench. Sophie had her bag on the ground instead of over one shoulder. Emily kept looking at the page under Rei’s arm. He had brought a new station roof for Marcus to complain about.
“Where is he?”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: “R-Rei. Can you come here?”
elements.speaker: emily

elements.text: “We didn’t want you hearing this in the corridor.”
elements.speaker: sophie

elements.text: He noticed Sophie’s voice before he understood the words. No invitation, no impatient joke about being late. He stopped just beyond her reach.
“Marcus died. His family told the school. He… he died by suicide.”
elements.speaker: emily

elements.text: The page bent against his ribs. For a moment all he could think was that he had brought the wrong thing. A roof. He had spent the evening drawing a roof while something had happened that made the whole morning impossible. Then the thought broke and Joseph’s face occupied the space it left.
“Where’s Joseph?”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: “Stay here.”
elements.speaker: sophie

elements.text: “Where is he?”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: Rei turned toward the buildings. Sophie stepped across his path. He tried to go around her, too fast; her bag caught under his shoe and he kicked it clear. The scrape made Emily flinch. He saw it and hated that he could still be moving.
“D-Don’t. Please, look at me.”
elements.speaker: emily

elements.text: “He kept doing it. He knew Marcus couldn’t—”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: He could not finish. His breath was arriving in short, useless pieces. There was a railing beside him and suddenly he was gripping it hard enough for the cold to hurt. He wanted something he could stop. A person he could put between his hands. Grief had no shape he knew how to fight.
“I’m angry too. You’re scaring us. Take your hands off that.”
elements.speaker: sophie

elements.text: “Move, Sophie.”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: “No. I’m not letting you run straight into him like this.”
elements.speaker: sophie

elements.text: “You can be angry here. I-I’m staying. But I can’t help you if you disappear.”
elements.speaker: emily

elements.text: Emily held out her hand without grabbing him. It shook. They had lost Marcus too, and he had made them spend their first words trying to keep him from hurting someone. The recognition reached him slowly, through the roaring in his ears. He let go of the railing.
“I should have been there.”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: “We don’t know everything he was carrying. I wish we did. That doesn’t mean you could have made him stay.”
elements.speaker: emily

elements.text: “I got you out. I got—”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: He stopped before he brought Yuriko into a school courtyard where her history did not belong. Emily knew the greenhouse. She did not know every room his mind had put beside it. In each of them there was someone he loved and a door he had reached either just in time or impossibly late.
“You don’t have to explain it properly. Sit down before you fall down.”
elements.speaker: sophie

elements.text: He sat. Emily sat beside him; Sophie stayed between the bench and the corridor until his gaze stopped searching past her. The storyboard lay closed on his knees. The next sob hurt more than the first because there was no anger in the way of it.
“He still has my pencil.”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: “I know.”
elements.speaker: emily

elements.text: “We’ll go to the counsellor together. In a minute. We can have a minute.”
elements.speaker: sophie

elements.text: They slowed him down that morning. They did not extinguish the anger; later it would find Joseph outside the administration entrance. For now Emily’s hand remained beside his, available without closing around it. He lowered his head and asked them to stay.
PRESENT — Rei’s home

His thumb was still caught on the folded paper. He flattened the corner, then stopped trying to flatten it. He remembered their fear as clearly as their kindness. He had wanted protection to mean that nobody close to him could ever be hurt. The impossible demand had survived the boy who first made it.
“Do you have somewhere in mind?” Sophie asked.
“No.”
“Good. I was going to pretend I did.”
Rei looked at her. She lifted one shoulder, and he felt the first small release of tension since leaving home.
They walked for a while without discussing why he had asked to meet. He noticed that she slowed when he did without making an announcement of it.
“You can walk normally,” he said.
“I am.”
“You're matching me.”
“That is normal when I'm walking with someone.”
He almost apologised. Instead he said, “I don't know what I want to talk about.”
“Then we can find out.”
“And if I don't?”
“We'll still have walked somewhere.”
A few steps later he said, “I remembered the bench.”
Sophie looked ahead. “Oh.”
He appreciated the smallness of the answer. She didn't ask him to describe everything.
“I thought I was remembering the film. Then I was back there.”
“Do you want to stop?”
“No. Keep walking.”
She did.
After a while she said, “I don't always know whether asking makes it worse.”
“It helps that you ask me.”
“All right.”
“And that you don't look disappointed when I don't know.”
Sophie gave him a brief sideways glance. “I have plenty of other things to be disappointed in. Your directions, for example.”
“We don't have a destination.”
“Exactly. Terrible planning.”
He laughed softly. They kept walking, and he did not have to explain the laugh either.

Sophie had to call his name twice at a crossing. He had been watching a dark vehicle turn into the next street and had not heard her first time. He apologised. She waited for him to actually look at her before continuing. The walk had no destination, but it still required him to be present for the person beside him.

Alone again, Rei remembered Joseph treating the bullying as something too small to answer for. The storyboard lay on the table in front of him. He let the present settle before following the memory farther.
FLASHBACK — Outside the school administration entrance
“Joseph.”
Joseph turned, impatience already on his face. “What?”
Rei had wanted him to turn. Now that he had, the words Rei had rehearsed no longer came in order.
“You don't get to talk about him like that.”
“Like what?”
“Like none of it mattered.”
Joseph looked toward the building. “I'm not doing this.”
“You took his things. You made everybody look. You waited until people were watching.”
“It was school. People get picked on.”
“His name was Marcus.”
“I know his name.”
“Then say it.”
Joseph tried to move past him. Rei stepped into his way.
“You think shouting at me changes anything?” Joseph said.
Rei wanted a reaction that would make the weeks of cruelty visible. He wanted Joseph to stop looking inconvenienced.
He shoved him against the wall and punched him. Joseph staggered and raised his arms. Rei lunged again before a teacher pulled him back.
“Rei. Step back. Now.”
“Let go.”
Another member of staff moved toward Joseph. Rei struggled once, then stopped when he realised he was still trying to reach him.
“You saw what he did,” he said. He was no longer sure who he was saying it to. “Where were you then?”
“We will take a statement about that. Right now, you attacked another student. You're coming to the office.”
Later, the suspension decision lay between him and the headteacher. His guardian would be contacted. There would be a return meeting. The bullying report would be addressed separately.
“So he gets to go back,” Rei said, “and act like it was nothing.”
“The suspension is for your actions today.”
He looked at his hand. It hurt. He had imagined Joseph's pain would make him understand something. He could not tell whether Joseph understood anything more than he had before.
Outside, Rei folded the letter around the unfinished storyboard. He walked away with both of them.
PRESENT DAY

He laid the remembered sequence beside the present feeling without pretending he was still in it. Being angry had not been the same as knowing what to do. He needed to remember that before deciding what came next.

At home that day, he had hidden the suspension paper beneath a schoolbook before Yuriko could see it. The concealment frightened him more afterward than the letter. He had wanted to be her safe person and had come home rehearsing excuses for hurting someone. The anger was his; the training had given it a fluent language. Adult Rei could remember both without calling either an acquittal.
Garrett put the clean towel down when Rei mentioned Marcus.
“The film?” he asked.
Rei nodded. “I keep coming back to it.”
“You told me about the bus timetable.”
“And the pigeon.”
“And the weather event.” Garrett's expression shifted into a small smile. “You sounded annoyed with him when you told me that part.”
“I was.”
“Good.”
Rei looked at him.
“I mean—” Garrett stopped. “That came out wrong.”
“No. I think I know.”
Garrett leaned back against the counter. “He gets to be somebody who annoyed you too. From the way you talk about him, I don't think he'd have made that difficult.”
Rei laughed, then looked down.
“I worry I'm telling the same story too often.”
“You haven't made me learn it for a test.”
“Garrett.”
“I don't mind hearing it.” The answer came without a joke this time. “I didn't know him. This is how I get to know something about him.”
Rei let that sit between them.
“Joseph still makes it small,” he said eventually.
Garrett's hands tightened briefly around the edge of the counter. “I remember you telling me.”
“I don't need you to do anything.”
“All right.”
The quick agreement surprised him.
“You can be angry,” Rei said.
“I am. I can be angry and stay here.”
Rei looked toward the unfinished cleaning. “You were working.”
“It'll wait.”
For once, Rei believed him without trying to calculate how much of a burden the waiting made him.

Garrett did not fill the pause. Rei almost used it to say he was fine. The answer was so familiar it had become a reflex, like moving a hand to cover an old scar. He let the silence last long enough to miss his chance. For once, someone else remained in the room without being asked to believe that he had everything under control.

Rei laid the storyboard across the table. Marcus had drawn three possible endings and crossed out only one. At school Rei had found that indecision irritating. Now he missed being able to tell him which ending was the worst.

Marcus had looked at his drawings before asking what he could do. No demonstration, no test of usefulness. At their first library table he had asked whether the sketched passenger was waiting for someone or resting. Rei had answered that he did not know. Marcus had said they could leave the passenger alone until he decided.

He had not known about the clan. That mattered too. Rei had been allowed to become a friend before becoming a history somebody felt obliged to handle carefully. He could be late, irritating, wrong about an ending. Marcus could sulk and come back with two versions. There had been room for both of them to be unfinished.
“You would hate how everyone gets sensible when I say your name.”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: The laugh escaped him, then failed halfway. He put the storyboard where he could see it without treating it as a set of instructions from the dead. He would not turn a friend’s drawings into evidence that he ought to have known.

Beside it lay two empty slots on an Iron Circle practice list. Jun, who used to lend him spare tape and complain about his handwriting. Luis, who stayed after bouts to help somebody else get their bag downstairs. Both had been offered Blackstone assessments. Neither had answered the private enquiries Rei had made after they stopped coming. They were people he knew, not names copied from a rumour.

Jun’s last ordinary message had included a picture of the public referral form and a complaint about how long the appointment would take. Nothing in it had sounded like goodbye. Rei had initially assumed work, an injury, a week away from the arena. Now an unanswered call could hold every absence he had ever lived through.

He had no proof of kidnapping yet. He had a document he could compare and a company he could ask. Joseph’s name made the decision hot and immediate; the thought of Jun and Luis gave it a direction beyond an old school wall. He took the referral reference to Blackstone.

RD16.title: The consent that was not there

elements.text: The receptionist’s desk was immaculate. Rei could see his reflection in the polished edge: someone who had dressed carefully enough to pass for calm. He had been awake most of the night. He had rehearsed an accusation on the way here and now could barely remember the polite version of the question.
“I’m asking about your assessment programme. Two people I know came here.”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: Robin could provide published participation information, not confirm private appointments. Rei knew why that distinction existed. Hearing it felt like being shut out of a room while somebody he knew was still inside.
“Then the public form. Please.”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: The project number matched Jun’s copy. A promise of performance assessment occupied most of the first page; withdrawal referred the reader to a separate security agreement. Rei ran a thumb under that sentence until the paper began to curl.
“This says they can leave. Where does it say what happens when they try?”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: Robin pointed to the public procurement reference for the archived agreement. She did not have the answer he wanted. He heard himself begin Joseph’s name in a tone that made her lean back, and stopped.
“Sorry. I need the reference. That’s all I’m asking you for.”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: Outside, he almost called Emily. He wanted her to answer immediately, to fill the space in which his mind had put her in the same building. Instead he looked at the unsent call and heard how frightened that would sound if he demanded to know where she was. She was Awakened too. That was a reason to tell her what he found, not a reason she owed him proof of safety every hour.

He photographed the form once, with the reference visible. The question for the archive was precise: did the security agreement permit Blackstone to hold somebody who had withdrawn? Underneath it, unhelpfully, ran another: if he had checked sooner, would Jun have answered?

The complaint described an assessment that did not end when the participant withdrew. The name was withheld. Rei kept it withheld as he compared the signed authorisation and the security contract. He had come looking for an explanation that left Jun and Luis somewhere ordinary. The documents kept removing those possibilities.

Richter had authorised restraint and continued weapons-response trials on Awakened people who tried to leave. The delivery records linked the project number to the loading compound, records office, experimental wing and executive command. Voluntary participation had become a recruiting phrase for a programme that withheld departure.

Jun’s voluntarily shared referral carried that same project number. Separately, a short account from Luis’s partner, supplied to Rei for the search, placed a Blackstone collection vehicle outside their building. Luis had said he was refusing further assessments. His bag was still at home. Taken together, the independent accounts and records described forced collection and confinement, not two competitors choosing to skip practice.

Rei left the partner’s address out of his working copy. He kept the original account and its source separate, for someone able to follow the disappearances. They were not going to become names scattered across an angry public accusation.
“They said no.”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: The words emerged too loudly. He read the authorisation again, looking for an exception that was not there. His foot had begun tapping beneath the table. He held it still with the other and found his hand had started instead.

He saw Jun handing a roll of tape to a nervous newcomer. Luis arguing that the arena stairs were a deliberate insult to injured knees. Then he saw Emily in the greenhouse years ago, and an empty bench, and Yuriko waiting for him to say she was safe. Different people, different rooms. His thoughts were beginning to force them into one demand: reach the door before it closes.

Emily’s awakening made the programme’s criteria personal in another way. He had no record naming her as a target. He knew that. Fear did not wait for her name to appear. Joseph had hurt people before and explained it away; now he had money, guards and rooms designed to keep someone inside.

Rei tried to write a sentence and found he had pressed through the paper. He put the pen away. A copied authorisation, the complaint, the referral match and the collection account were enough to establish the immediate work. He secured a duplicate of the evidence. Then he sat with his fists under the desk until he could stand without knocking the chair over.
He had begun the journal to keep fear separate from fact. Tonight it could still do that much. It could not make him sleep, or stop him hearing every unanswered call as the start of another loss.

RD18.title: A first draft, not a rescue

elements.text: “Can you read this?” Yuriko asked.
Rei reached for the pages. “Of course.”
“Actually read it.”
He looked up.
“Not the way you read something when you've already decided to tell me it's good.”
“I don't do that.”
“You get very quick at the end.”
He looked down at the draft, caught. “All right. I'll be slower.”
“That isn't exactly what I'm asking.”
He smiled and began again.
For a while she found small things to do elsewhere in the room. He could tell she was listening for the page turns. When he finished, she returned too casually.
“Well?”
“I understood what you were trying to do here.” He indicated a passage. “Then I wasn't sure why it changed.”
She frowned. “That was the part I liked.”
“You asked.”
“I know. I'm being gracious.”
“Very.”
She sat beside him and explained. He listened, then read the passage again.
“That isn't all on the page yet,” he said.
Yuriko looked annoyed for a moment, then thoughtful. “Will you read it when I change it?”
“Yes.”
“You don't have to promise immediately.”
“I want to.”
She gathered the pages, leaving the difficult one on top.
“Thank you.”
Rei had come into the room expecting to be asked how he was managing. It was a relief to have helped with something that belonged to her, and to know that helping had included disagreeing.

Rei caught himself trying to solve a crooked piece before Yuriko had decided whether she liked it that way. He drew his hand back. She was building a set, not asking him to prevent every possible collapse. The distinction should have been easy. His head was full of people he could not reach, and here was one small thing he could fix if he stopped listening.

RD19.title: The successor answers
RD19.chapter: Chapter 5 — A name is not an answer

elements.text: Rei heard the name of the organisation before he sat down.

The familiarity of it did not make the room familiar. He made himself look at what was actually there: three people waiting for his questions, records placed where he could read them, a chair he had not been ordered to occupy.
Emi spoke first.
“The name frightens you for a reason.”
He stayed standing a moment longer. “You don't know all the reasons.”
“No,” she said. “I don't.”
The admission was preferable to sympathy that claimed too much.
Ren moved the records toward him. “The current roster. The departure records. You can compare them with the filings.”
“Everyone here chose to come?”
“Adults only,” Emi said. “No child recruitment. No training through torture. Adults can leave.”
Rei sat and began reading. He did not want the conversation to make the documents unnecessary. They let him take the time.
When he looked up, Daichi was waiting.
“You kept the name,” Rei said.
“Yes.”
“Then you don't get to ask me to hear something different when you say it.”
“I haven't asked you to.”
“Not yet.”
Daichi accepted the correction without smiling. “What happened to you was wrong. I cannot make this place an answer to it.”
Rei looked back at the records. They matched the current filings. The evidence did not become less persuasive because he disliked what it required him to distinguish.
“And you would let me lead it?”
“I would relinquish command,” Daichi said. “Under that charter. You would be responsible for what happens here now.”
“That's a lot to put in front of someone with this history.”
“Yes.”
“Do you want me to make you feel forgiven?”
“No. I cannot ask you to call this home.”
Rei rested his hands on either side of the papers. He had expected to spend the meeting trying to make someone acknowledge the past. Now the past had been acknowledged, and the decision still hurt.

Daichi’s offer did not land as an honour. Rei heard an adult telling him what his strength could be used for, and the old pressure rose so quickly that he had to look away. This man had not given those orders. That did not prevent the likeness from making him sick. Ren waited with the departure records still open. The evidence required Rei to see a difference he did not yet know how to feel.

RD20.title: Outside Kurose House
RD20.chapter: Chapter 5 — A name is not an answer

elements.text: Outside Kurose House, Rei could still hear Ren saying that people left. Ren had not said it triumphantly. He had pointed to a dated departure, then another, and waited for Rei to read them. The ordinary patience was almost unbearable.

He wanted the name to have one meaning. If it did, he would know what to do with the shaking in his hands. Instead the present organisation had supplied evidence of voluntary adult membership, and the child in his head was still waiting for permission to stop.

A door closed behind him. He flinched and turned so sharply that a passing stranger stepped aside. No one had followed him. He looked back at the street, ashamed of the stranger’s startled face, then angry that he had another thing to be ashamed of.
“They’re gone.”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: He meant the original clan. Saying it had not changed the sound of the door. Leading this successor, leaving it or dismantling it would each affect living people who had not trained him. None could retroactively reach the boy in the training hall. He could know that and still want the sign torn off the building.

He rested his hands on the cold riverside rail. Jun and Luis were still missing. He had started counting exits at the archive and checking his phone in the middle of sentences. The danger at Blackstone was real. The certainty that every delay made him a bad brother, a bad friend, was becoming something he could barely question.

RD21.title: The decision is still yours
RD21.chapter: Chapter 5 — A name is not an answer

elements.text: “What would you want me to do?” Rei asked.
Emily looked at him for a long moment. “D-Do you want my answer, or a reason you won't have to be angry with yourself?”
He looked away. “That's a horrible question.”
“I know. I'm sorry.” She shifted her hands in her lap. “I don't mean you're trying to put it on me.”
“I might be. A little.”
She nodded. “I-I wish I could make it easier.”
“You don't have to say the right thing.”
“Good, because I don't know what it is.”
The honesty made him smile briefly.
Emily continued, “If you take responsibility, I want you to have room to be a person outside it. If you walk away, I don't want you to think that means you didn't face anything.”
“And if I make a choice you don't like?”
“I might tell you I don't like it.”
He looked at her again.
“I… I would still want to understand why,” she said.
Rei exhaled. He had not known how much he had been waiting for a promise of approval until she offered something less comfortable and more believable.
“You've asked me three different questions,” Sophie said. “Which one do you want to answer first?”
“I thought I asked what you think.”
“You asked whether you could do it, whether you should, and whether you'd regret it.”
“I'd like one answer that covers all three.”
“So would I. Very convenient.”
He rubbed a hand over his face, almost laughing.
Sophie leaned forward. “I think you should be allowed to want a life that isn't built around answering them.”
“That doesn't tell me what to choose.”
“No.” She paused. “I can stay while you work it out. I can't promise to make it painless.”
“What if I keep changing my mind?”
“Then tell me what changed. We can talk about that instead of starting the whole argument again.”

“I can’t explain the details,” Rei said.

His friend accepted the boundary. They could sit together without opening the file. He did not have to turn privacy into an excuse to leave.

Rei had been waking at every notification. Sometimes there was nothing on the screen; his hand had reached for the phone before he was fully awake. He did not want the person beside him to start organising their day around preventing that feeling. He also did not know how to ask them to stay without making their departure feel like a failure. The conversation had room for that difficulty, even when he could not name it neatly.

RD22.title: I will listen; I will still ask
RD22.chapter: Chapter 5 — A name is not an answer

elements.text: Garrett listened until Rei had finished the part he was willing to tell.
Then he said, “What do you want to be different when it's done?”
Rei looked at him. “I want it to be done.”
“I heard that.”
“Then why ask?”
“Because I don't know what done means here.”
Rei stared at the table. The question felt unfair because he had asked himself a version of it already and had not found an answer he liked.
“You think I'm doing this for the wrong reason.”
“I think you have more than one reason.” Garrett paused. “I do know what that feels like.”
Rei looked up again. Garrett did not explain the comparison. He simply stayed with the question.
“If I leave it alone, it still exists.”
“Yes.”
“If I take it on, it becomes something I have to keep answering for.”
“Yes.”
“You could be more helpful.”
“I could agree quickly. You'd notice.”
That earned a tired laugh.
Garrett lowered his voice. “I don't want to tell you something big enough to stop you hearing yourself. I can ask the irritating question and stay for the answer.”
“And if I don't have it tonight?”
“Then you eat before you try again.”

Rei looked at the food between them. He had begun the evening wanting someone to make his uncertainty feel unreasonable. Garrett was refusing to do that, which was annoying in exactly the way a best friend could afford to be.

The question followed him after the conversation: who would he be if there was nobody left to rescue tonight? He disliked it. He had once had an answer involving a sketchbook, a badly lit kitchen and time to waste. Lately he could not imagine wasting time without immediately seeing someone pay for it. That was not the same as having a purpose, however much it felt like one.

RD23.title: Accepting responsibility
RD23.chapter: Resolution A — What to do with the name

elements.text: “I'll do it,” Rei said.
Daichi waited rather than answering too quickly.
“Under the charter,” Rei added. “The parts about leaving. The parts about who doesn't get recruited. They don't become things we say because I'm in the room.”
“They remain the rules,” Daichi said.
“I want the records kept. I want to be able to see when something isn't working.”
Ren glanced at the existing papers. “We can begin with what is already documented.”
Rei nodded. Begin. He had been thinking about a decision as though its hardest part would be saying it.
Daichi relinquished command under the established conditions. Emi and Ren remained colleagues, not people whose private trust had been magically awarded to him.
When the meeting ended, Rei found himself with a question about an ordinary administrative detail. He asked it. Ren answered without treating it as a test of his right to be there.
Later, alone, he put the current papers away separately from the childhood notebook.

He had chosen work that would need doing tomorrow. That was what the decision had given him: responsibility, not ownership of the past. He was allowed to feel the weight of it without pretending certainty had arrived with the title.

Accepting did not quiet the boy who associated this name with pain. Rei could feel him in the impulse to turn a request into an order, to make every uncertain thing stand still. He would have to be accountable when that impulse appeared. Emi and Ren were colleagues with the right to disagree, not people whose obedience could prove he had become different.

RD24.title: Leaving without pretending
RD24.chapter: Resolution A — What to do with the name

elements.text: “I've read what you gave me,” Rei said. “I believe what these records establish about the current organisation.”
Daichi nodded.
“That doesn't make me want a place in it.”
“It doesn't have to.”
Rei had expected resistance. Without it, he almost continued arguing anyway.
“I don't want to be asked again because someone decides I need more time.”
“Understood.”
“And I am not telling you how to feel about that.”
Daichi's expression stayed measured. “You have given us an answer.”
Rei looked once more at the room. It would continue to exist when he left. There were people here who would have tomorrow's concerns without him being responsible for all of them.
Outside, he waited for the relief he thought should follow a boundary clearly stated. At first there was only tiredness.
Then he realised he could decide where to go next without returning to finish the conversation.
It was a small freedom, too ordinary to announce. He stood with it for a while before walking on.

He had expected leaving to feel larger. The street looked the same. A delivery driver wanted the pavement clear. Rei stepped aside and found that he could do that without giving the house any more of his life. The feeling in his chest came with him. Distance was something he could choose; relief would not necessarily arrive on command.

RD25.title: Choosing to dismantle
RD25.chapter: Resolution A — What to do with the name

elements.text: “I understand the distinction you're asking me to make,” Rei said. “I am not saying the original clan is still here.”
Daichi's face became more guarded.
“But I've decided to dismantle this organisation.”
There was a pause. Ren drew the current records closer.
“Then we disagree about what should happen to it,” Daichi said.
“Yes.”
Rei heard how little the word explained. There was no sentence he could add that would make the people in the room experience his choice exactly as he did.
He left with the decision made and the required actions still ahead. The organisation remained operational. He could not narrate an ending into existence because he had said what he intended.
The operations had closed. The staff survived and left their organisational duties. Rei recorded the outcome in plain language, then read it again.
He had wanted to know what would remain in him after the name no longer belonged to a functioning organisation he could approach. The answer did not arrive with the final victory.
He could still remember the timetable. The gaps were still gaps.

He sat until he could separate exhaustion from whatever else he was feeling. There would be time to describe it more accurately. For now he would not call the closure a restored childhood, or ask the people who had left to agree that it was.

He would not call the people who defended the successor his childhood captors. Their adult choices and their right to resent his decision remained real. Destroying the organisation could remove the sign and its operations. It could not turn every fear he carried into evidence that he had been right to do it.

RD26.title: One thread resolved
RD26.chapter: Resolution A — What to do with the name

elements.text: Rei returned to the separately kept programme records. Whatever he had chosen at Kurose House, these documents still described people prevented from withdrawing. He did not need to reopen his first decision to recognise the second task. He read the next location and checked what he actually needed before going.

The successor outcome was the last outstanding thread. Rei did not have to invent another immediate task because stopping felt unfamiliar. Home could be a place to pause, not the next problem to solve.

One decision was finished. His hands did not receive the news immediately. He kept finding them clenched while he stood still, as though they were waiting for the next obstruction. He opened them against his coat and felt the seam with each fingertip. Nothing about a resolved choice made the rest of the day simple.

RD27.title: Before you go
RD27.chapter: Resolution B — Before the executive door

elements.text: “D-Do you want us to ask you not to go?” Emily said.
Rei looked at her. “I don't know.”
“I don't know whether it would help either.” She rubbed her hands together. “I don't want to say something brave just because you're about to leave.”
Sophie leaned forward. “What can you actually tell us?”
“That I'm going alone. That I don't know how long it'll take.”
“Then don't give us a time you made up,” Sophie said.
He nodded.
Emily looked down, then back at him. “I-I'd like to see you afterward. That's what I want to say.”
“I'd like that too.”
“Not for a report.”
“I know.”
“And you don't have to be good company.”
Sophie glanced at her. “We were going to tell him that gently.”
Rei laughed despite himself. Emily smiled, then the smile faded into worry she did not try to hide.
“Please be careful,” she said.
He resisted the easy answer that would promise more than he could know.
“I'll pay attention.”
Sophie nodded. “Tell us when you're able. If we agree to wait somewhere, let's actually agree where. No guessing.”
They agreed he would let them know when he was able. Neither friend followed him into the operation. Their worry did not become a promise that everything would be all right.

His friends’ concern had become harder to wave away. The little pauses were accumulating: forgetting which question he was answering, arriving exhausted, looking past a familiar face toward the nearest door. He hated being watched for signs that he might come apart. He hated more that he had given them reason to watch.

He could hear how often protection had begun to sound like an instruction when it came out of his mouth. Go home. Don’t come here. Answer me. It was not the life he wanted to offer anyone. He wanted them safe and free, and fear kept telling him he could have only one.

RD28.title: A place to come back to
RD28.chapter: Resolution B — Before the executive door

elements.text: Garrett had listened without interrupting. That alone told Rei how much effort he was making.
“You're going to ask,” Rei said.
“Whether you want help?”
“Whether I'm sure.”
Garrett looked at the counter. “Would you believe me if I said I wasn't thinking it?”
“No.”
“Then I won't waste the line.”
Rei smiled faintly.
“I have to go alone.”
“All right.”
“You said that very quickly.”
“I can listen quickly. I'm talented.”
The joke gave them somewhere to stand for a moment.
Then Garrett said, “I don't like not knowing what happens after you leave.”
“I don't know either.”
“I know.” He took a breath. “That's the part I'm having trouble with.”
Rei looked at him. “I don't need you to make it easier to leave.”
“What do you need?”
He considered it.
“Don't make me explain everything when I come back.”
Garrett nodded. “Food first. Details if you want.”
“And if I don't?”
“Then we can have a very serious argument about dumplings.”
Rei felt his shoulders loosen.
“Save me something.”
“I can arrange that.”
The practical answer was easier to carry than a promise of safety. He left the conversation knowing there was somewhere he could arrive without having to begin with a successful ending.

Rei could picture returning here afterward. That made leaving harder, which surprised him. He had spent so long using attachment as a reason to move toward danger that he had forgotten it might also give him a reason to come back. Garrett would still be irritated if he vanished without a word. The thought mattered because it belonged to tomorrow.

RD29.title: The approach
RD29.chapter: Resolution B — Before the executive door

elements.text: Rei reached Blackstone with an evidence copy already secured elsewhere. That was the sensible part. He had told himself he would look at the entrance, check the route, give himself time to think. He had repeated the sentence all the way there.

Then a loading shutter came down. Metal struck concrete with a flat, final sound. Behind it were people who had tried to leave. In his head the sound became the training-hall door, the greenhouse, a call that never connected. He knew those events were different. He could no longer make knowing it slow his body down.

He called Jun once more. No answer. His thumb moved to Emily’s name before he stopped it. He had no evidence she was inside, no message saying she had been taken. The imagined picture was vivid enough to make him feel sick: Joseph deciding what her awakening was worth, Emily asking to stop, somebody noting the request and continuing.
“No. You don’t get another one.”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: He struck the wall beside the entrance. Pain ran up his arm. It did nothing useful; he hit it again before he could make himself stop. Breath caught in his throat and would not come cleanly. He bent over with his hands against his knees, furious at the tears, furious that he could not turn them into a plan.

For years he had made competence stand in for being all right. Get Yuriko out. Keep Emily safe. Win the bout. Make dinner. If the person beside him could breathe, he could postpone asking why he could not. Marcus had broken the bargain he had made with the world, because it had never been a bargain the world agreed to keep.

The part of him the clan had trained offered a familiar relief: stop thinking, find the obstruction, destroy it. It did not care about Jun’s jokes or Luis’s careful hands. Rei cared. At that moment he could barely separate caring from the urge to hurt the man who had taken them.

He wiped his face with his sleeve and moved toward the guard line before his breathing had settled. This was an attack born of anger and a breakdown, not a clean rescue plan. He would still have to survive each actual encounter and open the places where people were held. Rage supplied neither victory nor their safety.

RD30.title: Before the executive door
RD30.chapter: Resolution B — Before the executive door

elements.text: The executive door closed behind Rei. He heard it as a challenge. Joseph stood beyond the desk, intact and composed in a building full of people whose right to leave he had signed away. Rei threw the copied authorisation onto the polished surface hard enough to scatter the sheets.
“Where are Jun and Luis?”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: “If you mean programme participants, you have bypassed several proper channels.”
elements.speaker: Joseph Richter

elements.text: “They asked to leave. You collected one from his home. Don’t call that a channel.”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: Joseph looked at the scattered signature pages. His mouth tightened, then smoothed. Rei had seen that adjustment at school: the instant before cruelty dressed itself as somebody else’s misunderstanding.
“These are specialised trials. Interruption creates risks you are not qualified to assess.”
elements.speaker: Joseph Richter

elements.text: “You put them in restraints. You tested weapons on them. Say what you did.”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: He slammed a hand onto the desk. The sound startled even him. Joseph watched the hand, and Rei hated the small measuring look more than the evasion.
“You always did mistake losing control for having a point.”
elements.speaker: Joseph Richter

elements.text: “And you always found someone you thought couldn’t hit back.”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: “This is not school.”
elements.speaker: Joseph Richter

elements.text: “Marcus was not a rehearsal.”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: The name broke his voice. He had wanted to speak it steadily. Instead he saw a library table and an unfinished argument about an empty room. Marcus would never get to be tired of this conversation. Rei was so tired he could feel the effort of remaining upright.
“He made things. He wanted to finish a film. You made every room smaller for him and then acted like it was nothing. I can’t get him back. I know that. But you don’t get to keep doing this.”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: “You cannot lay an entire death at my feet.”
elements.speaker: Joseph Richter

elements.text: “I’m asking you to answer for what you chose. The bullying. The people locked downstairs. Your signature is right there.”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: Joseph’s sleeves parted around reinforced arms. A powered spinal frame locked into place. Targeting lights moved across the desk and found Rei. The machinery supplied the answer Joseph had been working toward: another advantage he could bring to an argument instead of listening.
“Awakened people take their advantages for granted. I built mine.”
elements.speaker: Joseph Richter

elements.text: “Is that what Emily would be to you? An advantage to take apart?”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: He had revealed the fear before he could swallow it. Joseph’s glance sharpened. Rei had no proof of a plan against her. He would not give Joseph another private detail to use.
“You brought that name into this room.”
elements.speaker: Joseph Richter

elements.text: “And it’s the last thing about her you’re getting from me.”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: His hands were shaking as he raised them. The boy trained to obey could have stood more neatly. The person he wanted to be would have recognised how close he was to making violence the answer to everything he could not bear. Both were here. Neither could do this for him.
“Open containment.”
elements.speaker: rei

elements.text: “Make me.”
elements.speaker: Joseph Richter

elements.text: Rei stepped forward, furious and frightened and past the point where he could pretend this was methodical. Joseph brought his weapons online. The confrontation would be decided by the fight, not by the force of either man’s words.

RD31.title: What an apology cannot return
RD31.chapter: Resolution B — Before the executive door

elements.text: The powered frame failed. The fight was over. Rei listened to the machinery falling silent.
Joseph spoke before Rei had decided what he wanted to say.
“I bullied Marcus. I chose to hurt him, and then pretended it didn't matter.”
Rei stood still.
“I am sorry,” Joseph said. “I am sorry for what I did to these people too.”
For years, Rei had imagined making him acknowledge it. He had never imagined the silence immediately afterward with any accuracy.
Marcus did not come into the room. The film remained unfinished. There were still people in this programme who needed the outcome to mean more than a conversation between two former classmates.
Rei secured the research records and disabled the containment controls. The surviving participants could leave.
Afterward, Rei noticed that he was still waiting to feel one clear thing. Relief and anger did not arrive in a useful order. He stopped trying to organise them before leaving.

“Not finished,” Rei said, looking at the unresolved objective when he was able. That was all he could accurately call it. He needed recovery and another assessment, not a story in which the confrontation had supplied closure.

Rei waited for the relief he had promised himself at the loading door. His breath still caught. Jun and Luis were among the surviving detainees: dazed, frightened, alive. When Jun recoiled from a sudden movement, Rei stopped approaching and let him choose the distance. Knowing someone from a ring did not give him the right to decide what that person needed now.

He had opened containment and secured the records. He could help people reach the exit and appropriate care. He could not promise their bodies would forget the rooms. He knew exactly how empty such a promise could be.

The urge to hit Joseph again returned after the apology. Rei stepped away from him instead, not because the urge was noble or because it had vanished, but because another blow would delay the living people waiting for help. Marcus did not become the price of this victory. Emily did not owe him gratitude for a threat he had feared on her behalf.

The failed attempt left his anger without the ending it had demanded. Retreat meant the programme was still unresolved. Resting, getting care and returning prepared would be harder for him than calling exhaustion courage. It was also the only way to make another attempt possible.

RD32.title: You came back
RD32.chapter: Resolution B — Before the executive door

elements.text: Sophie saw him before he worked out how to begin.
“Sit down,” she said, then stopped. “If you want. Sorry.”
“I want to.”
She moved a chair clear. He sat without making the movement look easier than it was.
“Do you need something now?”
“Water.”
She brought it and waited while he drank.
“The programme is stopped,” he said. Sophie nodded once. “All right.” She did not ask him to make that mean everything was finished.
“It isn't done,” he said. Sophie sat opposite him. “Then we don't have to pretend it is.”
He looked at the glass.
“I don't know what to say about it.”
“You already asked for water. That was useful.”
He gave a tired breath that almost became a laugh.
“I thought I'd be better at coming back.”
“There's no performance requirement.”
He looked up. Her face was serious despite the wording.
“Can we just sit?”
“Yes.”
For a while she stayed with him without checking whether the silence had improved him. Later she asked about food. He could answer that question too.

He did not have an account of the operation that made him sound composed. He could have edited it into one. Instead he let the pauses remain, and let the person beside him see how much of his strength had gone into getting through the door at all. Coming back was not the same as being well. It was the necessary beginning of letting anyone help.

RD33.title: The pages he keeps
RD33.chapter: Final chapter — A place in the present

elements.text: Rei put the old timetable and the current records on different parts of the table.
The distinction had become easier to describe. It had not become effortless to feel.

Tomorrow there would be questions from people whose present lives he had agreed to help govern. He would answer them as honestly as he could. The title did not entitle him to call uncertainty weakness in someone else.

The organisation would continue without his oversight. He did not need to invent a daily obligation to check whether leaving had been the correct decision. He had read, asked and chosen. That history belonged in the record too.

The successor's operations were closed. The original childhood still could not be revised. He could record the closure without demanding it produce one particular feeling every time he thought about it.

The Blackstone programme was stopped. Joseph had acknowledged what he had done. Rei kept the acknowledgement in its actual place: something that had happened, not a replacement for what had happened before it.
He opened the storyboard once more. The pigeon was still on the page.
“I'm keeping this,” he said.
There was no one there who needed convincing. He could put it away and return to it another day. He could draw something else without asking whether that meant he had forgotten.
For now, he cleared enough room on the table to begin.

The investigation journal had served its purpose: dates, sources, names kept out of careless circulation. He did not need to manufacture another entry to justify putting it away. On a separate page he wrote an ordinary task for himself: arrange support for the sleep he had been losing and the fear he kept disguising as responsibility. Then he left space for an actual appointment, not a promise that he would handle it alone.

He still wanted to protect people. He wanted to make dinner and draw and disagree about a film ending too. The weapon the clan had raised did not vanish when he chose those things. It ceased, for one evening, to be the only account of what his hands were for.

RD34.title: The next ordinary evening
RD34.chapter: Final chapter — A place in the present

elements.text: Garrett gave Rei a job small enough that he suspected it had been selected carefully.
“You can tell me if you just want company,” Rei said.
“I also want those folded.”
“You've given me three.”
“High standards. Start small.”
Rei sat down with the wrappers. Garrett worked beside him, occasionally glancing over without correcting him.
“Are you going to say anything?” Rei asked.
“About the folding?”
“About anything.”
Garrett put down what he was holding.
“I was trying not to ask for a report.”
“You can ask how I am.”
“All right. How are you?”
Rei looked at the little row he had made.
“I don't know yet.”
Garrett nodded. “That's an answer.”
“Not a very helpful one.”
“It tells me not to decide for you.”
Rei sat with that for a moment. Then he asked, “How was your day?”

Garrett began to answer lightly, stopped, and told him about an ordinary irritation instead. Nothing in the account needed to become a clue. Rei listened, disagreed with one small detail, and found himself defending the disagreement with more energy than he expected.
Garrett grinned. “There you are.”
Rei looked down. “I was here before.”
The grin softened.
“Yeah,” Garrett said. “You were. Sorry.”
Rei nudged the tray toward him. “These are better than your first one.”
“Historically inaccurate.”
“You kept the evidence.”
Garrett laughed. Rei let himself enjoy having the last word for as long as it lasted.

He stayed after the meal without inventing a reason to be useful. The bowls could wait a little. Garrett did not need a rescue, and Rei did not need to earn the chair by providing one. It felt unfamiliar enough that he almost stood anyway. He kept sitting.

RD35.title: A place in the present
RD35.chapter: Final chapter — A place in the present

elements.text: Yuriko put her revised pages down beside Emily's materials.
“No one is allowed to call this a productive afternoon,” Sophie said.
“W-Why?” Emily asked.
“Because then someone will give me a task.”
Rei passed her the nearest light object that needed moving. “Too late.”
Sophie looked at it, then at him. “I trusted you.”
“You arrived.”
“A terrible mistake.”

Yuriko laughed and shifted the papers out of the way before anyone spilled something on them. Emily asked about the revision. For a while the conversation belonged to the two of them, and Rei found himself listening without waiting for his turn to explain how he was doing.
When Yuriko asked him about the changed passage, he read it again.
“That makes more sense.”
“Do you like it?”
“Yes.”
“You can say both things at once, you know.”
“I'm trying not to be too quick at the end.”
She smiled at the callback. Emily looked between them but didn't ask for an explanation.
Later, Sophie began proposing something for another day. Emily objected to the timing. Yuriko wanted to finish her draft first. Rei listened to them negotiate a plan that did not yet exist.
“What about you?” Sophie asked.
He realised he had been thinking about being invited rather than about whether he could come.
“Ask me again when you've agreed what it is.”
“Very demanding.”
“I've learned from all of you.”
They argued a little longer. Nothing in the room required him to turn the afternoon into proof that he was healed.
When he reached for a fresh page, he was thinking about what he wanted to put on it.

When he noticed himself checking the door, he returned his attention to the unfinished piece on the table. The people he loved were not proof that he had succeeded at keeping the world harmless. They were people, with evenings and preferences that belonged to them. He listened to the next small disagreement and let it matter on its own scale.

FD01.title: Before opening
FD01.chapter: Chapter 1 — The street before the file

elements.text: Fox noticed the shopkeeper checking the street before turning the sign. He knew the difference between looking for customers and waiting for somebody one did not want to see. It was a useful observation, not yet an explanation. He kept the thought to himself until the person chose to speak.

Gordon had questions prepared. He put them aside long enough to ask whether this was still a good time. A person agreeing yesterday did not become obliged to be ready today, particularly with two investigators standing in the doorway.
“Do you want to do this here?” Gordon asked.
The shopkeeper looked toward the counter. “I need to open.”
“We can keep out of the way,” Fox said.
“You say that. People notice you.”
Fox glanced toward Gordon. “Mostly him.”
The shopkeeper almost smiled, then did not.
Gordon moved away from the centre of the entrance. “We can arrange another time. You decide whether to give an account.”
“I want it stopped. I don't want everyone deciding I've started something.”
“Tell us what actually happened,” Gordon said. “We won't ask you to answer for the whole street.”
The shopkeeper took out the three demands, but kept a hand on them.
“And tomorrow?”
Neither man answered immediately.
“Tomorrow still matters,” Fox said.
“That isn't a promise.”
“No.” He looked at the papers. “It's why we're asking about the contact route as well as the collector.”

The shopkeeper let go of the documents one at a time. The dates were supplied willingly. Gordon checked how each copy had been retained, and Fox listened without turning every uncertain phrase into a reason to interrupt.

Behind the counter, a cup had been left beneath the leaking coffee machine. One drop fell, then another. The shopkeeper kept looking at it without moving to empty it. The ordinary work of opening had become a list of things that could wait until two dangerous men left the room.
“You don't have to like us. You don't even have to think this'll work.”
elements.speaker: fox

elements.text: “You should know what we're offering before you decide. Someone you can reach after we leave. A response if the collector returns. We start there.”
elements.speaker: gordon

elements.text: Fox listened to the traffic outside. Somewhere a delivery driver was losing an argument with a shutter. The city would continue selling breakfast while someone was beaten behind the next building. He had once mistaken that indifference for peace. Now he trusted the sound of a street only after he had checked what it concealed.

Gordon could promise neither a quiet city nor a permanent guard at every door. It would have been easy to make honesty sound like an excuse for doing very little. He wanted the shopkeeper to leave this conversation with something useful: one person who would answer, and an agreed next step small enough to be kept.

FD02.title: The same doorway
FD02.chapter: Chapter 1 — The street before the file

elements.text: At the back of the shop, Gordon stopped short of the threshold.
“Street side?” he asked Fox.
Fox looked past him. “If you're staying with the account.”
“Yes.”
It was a small exchange, complete in a few words. The doorway recalled a time when neither had understood what the other was trying to protect.

The doorway caught Fox's attention for a reason he did not immediately give. It framed a narrow passage, a person waiting behind somebody stronger, the point at which an argument could become a trap. Gordon had learned to notice when Fox stopped looking at the room and began measuring an older one against it.
“You're doing it again.”
elements.speaker: gordon

elements.text: “Checking the exit isn't a nervous habit.”
elements.speaker: fox

elements.text: “I didn't call it one.”
elements.speaker: gordon

elements.text: Fox rubbed the raised seam on his glove. When Gordon had first stood between him and a suspect, he had taken it as a challenge from a man who had never needed to be afraid. He had been wrong about the second part. Gordon was afraid of plenty. He simply refused to let fear decide who stopped being a person.
“First time we met, I thought you'd last a week.”
elements.speaker: fox

elements.text: “I thought you might eventually stop saying that.”
elements.speaker: gordon

elements.text: “Neither of us is getting everything he wants.”
elements.speaker: fox

FM01.title: The same doorway, years not specified
FM01.chapter: Chapter 1 — The street before the file

elements.text: FLASHBACK — A separate earlier Blackhaven witness-protection incident

Fox had followed a physical lead into the lane. Finding an officer between him and the next turn felt like arriving just in time to be told he was too late. He noticed the uniform before he noticed the worker waiting behind it, and later would remember that order with irritation.

Gordon had a person waiting to leave and an unfamiliar armed man approaching. He could not afford to treat confidence as authorisation. He also could not afford to ignore the way the man had stopped speaking to listen toward the bend.
“Hold there,” Gordon said.
“I need that lane.”
“Then tell me why.”
Fox looked beyond the doorway. “Somebody stopped around the turn.”
“Somebody?”
“Footsteps. Then nothing. Close enough that I would check before taking anyone out.”

Gordon changed his angle and checked. He did not announce that the sound proved an offence. The worker behind him moved forward, then stopped when another person visibly tried to obstruct the departure.
Fox stepped toward the lane.
“Not past me,” Gordon said.
“I'm looking at the obstruction.”
“And I have somebody trying to get out.”
Fox looked behind him properly for the first time.

A brief silence. Then he moved to the street-facing position rather than farther into the lane. Gordon escorted the worker clear while Fox held the street-facing position. The worker cleared the lane; that was the part Fox could see.
When the immediate danger had passed, Fox turned back.
“You could have said you were moving someone.”
“You could have asked before choosing the direction.”
“Would you have told me?”
“Enough to keep you out of the doorway.”
Fox gave a short breath that was not quite a laugh.
“You did check.”
“You gave me something worth checking.”
“That sounded painful to admit.”
“It was less painful than ignoring it.”
Neither offered friendship. They had an account to compare and a person whose safety did not become less important because they had begun arguing.

Fox remembered the young officer's posture more clearly than the first words. He had expected somebody who wanted obedience. Instead Gordon had kept looking past him toward the person caught behind their disagreement. It had been insulting to discover that Fox was not the most important thing in the doorway.
“You planning to stand there until I calm down?”
elements.speaker: fox

elements.text: “I'm planning to stand here until they can leave.”
elements.speaker: gordon

elements.text: The answer had annoyed him because it supplied a measurable end to an argument he had wanted to win. It was possible to step aside without admitting every part of his anger was wrong. It was also possible for the officer to remain afraid and still refuse to move.
Fox had worked for men who required admiration before they would offer help. This one seemed prepared to accept his dislike. He did not call that courage at the time. He remembered it anyway.
PRESENT DAY
He took the agreed position. Gordon no longer had to explain the doorway to him, but Fox still wanted the question asked rather than the answer assumed.
PRESENT DAY

The brief acknowledgment from Fox let Gordon return to the shopkeeper without looking over his shoulder to guess where his partner had gone. It was cooperation built out of something they had once done badly.

FD03.title: Terms of help
FD03.chapter: Chapter 1 — The street before the file

elements.text: The shopkeeper pointed to a date.
“That was the second demand. I paid the first because I thought perhaps it would end.”
Fox looked up. “Did they say it would?”
“Not in those words.”
Gordon waited while the shopkeeper considered the distinction.
“I wanted it to mean that,” they said.
Fox nodded once. “All right.”

There were copies of three demands and an account of repeated pressure. No confession from an entire organisation. Gordon stated the difference in the record without making the person repeat the frightening part for emphasis.
Outside the conversation, Fox spoke more quietly.
“We know the point they use. Waiting has a cost.”
“So does acting on an incomplete route,” Gordon said.
“I didn't say wander in.”
“No. Tell me what you want to check first.”
Fox indicated the physical comparison he wanted to make. Gordon described the documentation and protected contact arrangement still needed.
It helped that Gordon asked for the next action instead of asking him to become a more patient person. Fox could explain an action. He could not promise never to resent the waiting.
Fox's urgency was not an obstacle to be removed from the plan. It identified the point at which the plan might become an excuse for delay. Gordon still needed the route corroborated, and said so.

They divided the immediate work explicitly. The shopkeeper was told what they could expect next and what remained uncertain. No one promised that handing over papers would make tomorrow safe by itself.
“If stopping him means he doesn't get up again, I can live with that.”
elements.speaker: fox

elements.text: “I need you to hear the whole instruction. Stop the threat. If he can be taken alive, we take him alive.”
elements.speaker: gordon

elements.text: “And when that costs somebody else?”
elements.speaker: fox

elements.text: “Then I answer for the decision I actually make. I won't give you permission for every possible killing before we've met the man.”
elements.speaker: gordon

elements.text: There was no raised voice. That made the disagreement harder to dismiss as temperament. Fox looked through the glass at a customer counting coins. For him the arithmetic was brutal and uncomplicated: leave one predator able to act, and strangers paid for the restraint. He did not consider the stranger's suffering more acceptable because nobody had signed an order for it.
“I'm here because it might stop the next demand. Don't mistake that for faith in your book.”
elements.speaker: fox

elements.text: “You can distrust the book. You still have to work with the person holding it.”
elements.speaker: gordon

elements.text: Fox gave him the smallest acknowledgment. It was an agreement about this operation, not a conversion.

FD04.title: The wrong familiarity
FD04.chapter: Chapter 2 — A trace is not a person

elements.text: The chemical note was there. Fox recognised it before he finished crossing the accessible frontage. The difficulty began when recognition tried to turn itself into a conclusion.

Gordon trusted Fox's report of the trace. He did not yet know how many perfectly ordinary places the same report could describe. Asking that question felt more delicate than it should between two people who claimed to value accuracy.
“The envelope and that entrance,” Fox said.
“You're confident?”
“In the trace.”
Gordon looked along the frontage. “How many other doors could it put us at?”
Fox's expression tightened. “You think I imagined it.”
“No. I think we need to know how specific it is.”

A consenting worker identified a routinely used cleaner. With permission, they compared the labelled product, the supply record and other accessible surfaces. The same broad note appeared in more than one ordinary place.
Fox stood beside the original entrance again.
“Common product,” he said.
“Yes.”
“Not a unique source.”
Gordon wrote that down without adding a correction in a different voice.
Fox looked at him. “You can leave the observation in.”
“I was going to.”
The more specific fibres and the observed collection route still mattered. They checked those instead of discarding everything because the first inference had been too large.
Naming the limit himself felt better than defending a claim he no longer believed. It did not make the lost certainty pleasant.
He made sure the record credited the useful observation. An accurate correction did not require making his partner smaller.

Fox hated losing a lead more when it felt familiar. The scent had arrived with the comfort of recognition: there, that one, move. His body had begun preparing for pursuit before the comparison caught up. Eight Senses supplied more of the world than most people could bear to notice. They did not explain why a man was in it.
“I wanted it to be him.”
elements.speaker: fox

elements.text: “I know.”
elements.speaker: gordon

elements.text: “That's not an apology for checking. It's why I'm checking twice.”
elements.speaker: fox

elements.text: Gordon kept the discarded inference beside the useful observation instead of letting the correction become a lecture. A false certainty could send Fox toward somebody's throat. It could also send a signed Interpol order to the wrong home. The distinction between their methods did not exempt him from the same temptation.
“We have a route worth checking. That's progress.”
elements.speaker: gordon

elements.text: “You've got a very forgiving definition.”
elements.speaker: fox

elements.text: “A person we didn't accuse is allowed to count.”
elements.speaker: gordon

FD05.title: The person at the counter
FD05.chapter: Chapter 2 — A trace is not a person

elements.text: Before the collection encounter, the shopkeeper looked toward the exit they had discussed.
“If I need to stop talking?”
“Stop,” Gordon said. “Tell us what you need.”
Fox checked the actual approach. “You don't have to keep somebody interested for our benefit.”
The collector had not agreed to stop. The opposition on this route would have to be faced before the witness could be safe from this demand.

He had wanted the next step to come quickly. Now it was here, with somebody else standing close enough to live with its consequences. He kept that person in his actual assessment of the scene rather than treating the target as all that mattered.
A plan looked cleaner when nobody had begun to move. Gordon checked the partner beside him. Writing the preparation had not finished his part in it.
At the headquarters review, the shopkeeper’s last question remained with them. “Can I close?” The answer they had given belonged in the account too.
Gordon checked what they had secured before answering. The seized receipt supplied a rail-yard lead. It did not give him a reason to keep a tired witness talking indefinitely.
Fox moved out of the person's way.
“We'll tell you what comes next,” Gordon said. “Through the route we agreed.”
“And if nothing comes next?”
“Then you still hear from us about this report.”
The promise would require follow-through. Gordon wrote the agreed route beside the report, where he would have to see it again.

The collection point was too ordinary for the amount of preparation it required. A counter edge worn smooth by hands. A bell over the door. Fox could imagine how quickly the room would fill with the noise of a struggle, and how long the shopkeeper would hear that bell differently afterward.
“Stay behind me when it starts.”
elements.speaker: fox

elements.text: “Give them the route out. Don't make yourself the route.”
elements.speaker: gordon

elements.text: Fox shifted half a step. He disliked being corrected in the few seconds before violence; he disliked more that Gordon was right. Standing closest to danger could become its own vanity. The person they were protecting needed an open passage, not a demonstration of how much punishment he could take.
“If he reaches for them, I'm ending it.”
elements.speaker: fox

elements.text: “Stop him. I'll cover the exit.”
elements.speaker: gordon

elements.text: The answer left the disagreement intact. Both men checked the door again. Neither could make the next minute safe by finding a better sentence for it.

Back at the review table, Fox remembered the bell most clearly. Not the impact or the moment the collector's pressure broke: the bell moving afterward, ridiculous and delicate in the sudden quiet. It was difficult to explain how such a small noise could make him angrier than a threat.
“He'll be somebody's cousin. Somebody will tell us he wasn't always like that.”
elements.speaker: fox

elements.text: “They may be telling the truth.”
elements.speaker: gordon

elements.text: “Doesn't help the person he hurt.”
elements.speaker: fox

elements.text: “No. Neither does pretending he was born with a demand letter in his hand. We can stop what he did without making up the rest.”
elements.speaker: gordon

elements.text: Fox left the argument there. Gordon had not asked the witness to forgive anybody. That mattered more to him than the careful language in the file.

FD06.title: Names after the report
FD06.chapter: Chapter 2 — A trace is not a person

elements.text: The report linked the collection cell to the Lantern Crew. Gordon left the wording narrow.
Fox read the relevant line. “Not every member.”
“Not from this evidence.”
“Good.”
Gordon looked up briefly, then continued.
They reviewed the protected contact route and the actual receipt. The next lead was real, but neither had to leave the room before the first case had been described accurately.
Watching Gordon make room for his observations in the account brought back the first time he had expected the uniform to mean his contribution would be edited out.
Fox's attention to the wording reminded him of the first debrief, when every distinction had sounded like a personal slight. It had taken more than a clever answer to change that.

Gordon loosened the strap across his shoulder. The red pressure mark beneath it would be gone by morning. The shopkeeper would still be deciding whether the next footstep outside meant trouble. It was an uncomfortable difference between doing an operation and living where it had happened.
“Don't give them your cheerful voice next time.”
elements.speaker: fox

elements.text: “I wasn't aware I had one.”
elements.speaker: gordon

elements.text: “The one that says you can go home afterward.”
elements.speaker: fox

elements.text: Gordon considered that without defending his tone. He had meant to reassure. Fox had heard distance. Neither intention nor interpretation could settle what the shopkeeper had heard.
“I'll ask how the arrangement is working. Then I'll listen.”
elements.speaker: gordon

elements.text: “There. Better.”
elements.speaker: fox

elements.text: Fox stayed while Gordon made the practical arrangement. He could despise paperwork and still recognise the use of a name attached to a promise. Anonymous concern had failed too many people to deserve his respect.

FM02.title: An introduction after the noise
FM02.chapter: Chapter 2 — A trace is not a person

elements.text: FLASHBACK — Later on the day of their first meeting, then a separately marked later appointment
“Jeremy Gordon,” the officer said.
“Fox.”
“Your account of the lane?”
Fox gave it, briefly. Gordon made notes.
“That's not what I said,” Fox interrupted.
Gordon turned the page so he could read it. “Which part?”
“You've separated the sound from the person.”
“You heard movement before we saw the obstruction.”
“And then there was an obstruction.”
“Yes. Those are two observations supporting the account. I haven't removed either.”
Fox read again.
Gordon added that Fox had changed position to protect the departure. He did not describe the worker's destination.
“So you can put the useful part in,” Fox said.
“That was the intention.”
“You missed the blind bend in your route check.”
Gordon looked at the line he had written about the approach. He amended it.
Fox waited for the amendment to become an argument about his manners. It did not.

The small correction unsettled him more than a defensive speech would have. He knew how to distrust somebody who never admitted being wrong. He had less practice with somebody who could admit it without making a show of virtue.
He did not enjoy having the omission pointed out. Enjoyment was not the criterion. Fox had seen something useful, and an accurate account was worth the discomfort of retaining it.
“Delivery traffic changes this lane,” Fox said. “At another hour, your clear approach isn't clear.”
“Can you show me?”
Fox looked at him. “You?”
“Yes.”
They agreed on a later time. No clearance, private file access or formal appointment as an associate was granted by the exchange.
Gordon arrived himself. Fox was already there.
“You came,” Fox said.
“We agreed.”
“I expected someone carrying your questions.”
“I can carry them.”

Fox led him through the accessible route. Gordon asked about a physical detail, listened to the answer and checked what it would mean at the actual departure time. Fox did not have to exaggerate the usefulness of the detail to keep his attention.
At the doorway, Gordon stepped aside before Fox asked.
“Learning,” Fox said.
“From a demanding instructor.”
It was the first remark Fox did not feel obliged to challenge.

The introduction afterward had felt unnecessary to Fox. They knew the relevant things already: one man would act, the other would interfere. Gordon had nevertheless offered his name as though the next meeting did not have to be a repetition of the first.
“You always start over this politely?”
elements.speaker: fox

elements.text: “Only when I expect to see someone again.”
elements.speaker: gordon

elements.text: Fox had looked at the cup instead of taking that seriously. He was unused to being offered a future encounter that was neither a contract nor a threat. There was no reason to become sentimental about an officer being civil. He supplied his own name, curtly enough to disguise the decision as impatience.

Gordon used it without a nickname or a warning. Later, Fox would remember that too: the small relief of hearing his name mean only that someone wanted his attention, and the immediate suspicion that came after relief.
PRESENT DAY
Fox set the current rail receipt beside the completed report. “I'll come for the next check.” Gordon nodded. Neither named the offer loyalty. Both knew it had not been automatic at the beginning.

FD07.title: Two ledgers
FD07.chapter: Chapter 3 — The number on the crate

elements.text: The number matched. Gordon put the receipt beside the ledger entry, aligning the fields.
“There,” he said.
